analysis.one_liner: Lets retirees keep their company health benefits while courts review cuts, and makes employers prove promises were never made.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died in the Senate Labor Committee at the end of the 104th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company cuts or ends health benefits for its retirees, the retirees can sue. This bill would have rewritten the rules of that lawsuit to favor retirees: courts would have to order the company to keep paying the benefits while the case is pending, with no bond required from retirees. If the plan paperwork was silent or unclear about whether benefits could be cut, the employer would have to prove it warned retirees clearly, at least 90 days before retirement, that the benefits could end. It also let unions and retiree representatives sue on retirees' behalf. The bill was introduced with bipartisan support but never advanced out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and disabled former employees whose company health benefits are being cut or eliminated, plus their spouses and dependents. Under the bill, their benefits would stay in place while a court decides the case, they would not have to post money to get that protection, and unclear plan documents would count in their favor. Unions and retiree organizations could file suit for them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Retirees facing cuts to company health benefits

how_it_helps.text: Courts would have to order employers to keep retiree health benefits at their previous level while a lawsuit over the cut is pending, with no bond or other security required from the retiree, and the order could be lifted only on clear and convincing evidence that the case is meritless.

If the summary plan description or retirement materials were silent or ambiguous about whether benefits could be cut after retirement, the burden shifts to the employer to prove it distributed materials at least 90 days before retirement that did not promise lifetime benefits and clearly disclosed that benefits could be cut, in language an average participant could understand.
Employee representatives, such as unions, could bring or appear in these lawsuits on behalf of retired employees, their spouses, and dependents.
The rules would apply retroactively to cases pending or filed on or after March 23, 1995, so retirees whose benefits had just been cut could use them.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and plan sponsors that provide retiree health benefits. They would keep paying benefits during litigation, carry the burden of proof when plan documents are unclear, and face suits brought by unions and retiree representatives. Plan sponsors that cut benefits in step with current-employee cuts or managed-care changes would be exempt.

drawbacks.text: The mandatory continuation order would require employers to keep paying benefits for the full length of litigation, which for a financially struggling company could add significant cost even if it ultimately prevails.

Employers already lost a major case on this issue before the bill was introduced: in 1994 the Supreme Court ruled in Curtiss-Wright Corp. v. Schoonejongkenh that ambiguous retiree benefits documents must be construed against the employer, so critics argued some of the bill's burden-shifting already existed in the courts.
The retroactive effective date would apply new litigation rules to cases already pending, changing the rules mid-dispute for employers and retirees alike.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered real, concrete protection to a vulnerable group: retirees who were promised or expected lifetime health coverage and saw it cut. The main cost falls on plan sponsors, who would pay benefits during litigation and bear a heavy disclosure burden when their documents are unclear. The exemptions for cuts matching those made to current employees and for managed-care changes limited the burden on employers adjusting to the managed-care era. It was a targeted litigation-rules bill, not a broad mandate, but the continuation requirement and retroactivity were real costs for employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never acted on it, so it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tom Daschle introduced the Retiree Health Benefits Protection Act on March 22, 1995, joined by Sens. Harkin, Wellstone, and Pressler.
Five senators cosponsored the bill: four Democrats and one Republican.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on March 22, 1995.
No further action was taken; the bill never received a committee markup, a floor vote, or House consideration before the Congress ended in January 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and plan sponsors that retiree health benefits were cut or eliminated in the mid-1990s kept full discretion to do so without the bill's continuation orders and burden-of-proof rules, and no comparable protection for retirees became law in that Congress.

for.name: Sen. Tom Daschle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: Sens. Harkin, Wellstone, and Pressler
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Sen. Nancy Kassebaum
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or committee vote on the bill during the 104th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was mostly Democratic with one Republican (Sen. Pressler of South Dakota) among the original cosponsors, but the decisive inaction was the Republican-run committee never scheduling the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to keep paying contested retiree benefits during litigation and shifted the burden of proof to them when plan documents are unclear. Its death left them free to cut or terminate retiree health benefits with the pre-existing, employer-friendlier litigation rules.

industries.industry: Managed care organizations and utilization review firms
industries.note: The bill exempted benefit changes tied to adding managed care, utilization review, or provider restrictions, so employers shifting retirees into managed-care arrangements would not trigger the continuation requirement. This carved out room for the managed-care model while still covering outright terminations.
